conventions.convention: Measurement spaces are nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces; outcome sets are finite and nonempty. Zero outcome projections and zero effects are permitted.
The root complex inner product is linear in its first argument. POVM weights are tr(ρ E_a); the effects alone do not prescribe conditional output states.
The density set carries the subspace topology and Borel σ-algebra from real and imaginary matrix entries in a fixed ordered basis; every subset of the finite outcome set is an event.

Complete positivity quantifies over every integer ancilla dimension r ≥ 1, with the ancilla last and amplification acting entrywise on its operator blocks. The r = 1 map is identified with the original map through canonical unitary identifications.

An instrument has nonzero input space, finite-dimensional output space, completely positive complex-linear branches, and total trace preservation on every input operator. Conditional output is divided by its weight only when that weight is positive; at zero weight its value is the nonstate symbol ⊥.

Naimark outcome labels are converted to numeric register indices by an arbitrary fixed bijection j; |a⟩ means e_{j(a)}. The conclusion is an algebraic isometric compression, without an implementation claim.

load_bearing.statement: A finite instrument consists of completely positive complex-linear branch maps whose output traces sum to the input trace for every input operator. Its conditional state is the branch output divided by its weight when positive, and ⊥ when the weight is zero.
A finite POVM on nonzero finite-dimensional H is a family of nonnegative endomorphisms E_a indexed by a finite nonempty set, with sum I_H. Its density-operator outcome weights are p_ρ(a) = tr(ρ E_a).
A complex-linear map Φ is completely positive if, for every finite r ≥ 1, its block amplification Φ^(r) sends every nonnegative operator on H ⊗ C^r to a nonnegative operator on K ⊗ C^r.

For finite-dimensional complex H,K and r ≥ 1, every operator on H ⊗ C^r has unique ancilla blocks X_ij. For every complex-linear Φ:L(H)→L(K), the rule [X_ij]↦[Φ(X_ij)] defines a unique well-defined linear amplification; at r = 1 it is Φ under the canonical unitary identifications.

Let ρ be a density operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space H, and let (P_a) be a finite projective measurement on H. Then tr(ρ P_a) lies in [0,1] for every a, and the weights sum to one.
For a density operator ρ on nonzero finite-dimensional complex H and a finite POVM (E_a), every tr(ρ E_a) belongs to [0,1], and their sum is one.
For a finite POVM (E_a) on H and its nonnegative square roots M_a = E_a^(1/2), the maps I_a(X) = M_a X M_a form an instrument from H to itself.
For a finite instrument and an input density operator ρ, if tr(I_a(ρ)) = 0, then I_a(ρ) = 0 and the conditional value is ⊥, not a density operator.

concerns.concern: Proof 1.1 writes Q_a(x ⊗ e_c) = δ_{a,c} x ⊗ e_a and later uses δ_{a,c}δ_{a,d}. The Statement allows arbitrary outcome labels a ∈ Ω and defines |a⟩ = e_{j(a)} for a bijection j:Ω→{0,…,r−1}; thus e_a and comparison of a with numeric c are not defined in general. The intended formula uses δ_{j(a),c} and e_{j(a)}. The subsequent compression argument uses j correctly.

alerts.finding: Facts [F4] attributes to def-qc-povm-and-outcome-law: “measuring a two-outcome projective flag and ignoring the unmeasured data register yields the corresponding compressed effect on the input.” The cited Definition gives nonnegative effects summing to identity and weights tr(ρ E_a); it contains no dilation or compression assertion. Proof 3.1 uses [F4] to identify the circuit effect as V_00* V_00. That identification needs the short trace-cyclicity calculation for the initialized flag, rather than this stronger restatement of the cited Definition.

Proof 2.1 says: “In the orthonormal eigenbasis from step 1.1, the matrix of T is diagonal with those nonnegative real eigenvalues on the diagonal. Thus claim 2 implies claim 3.” Step 1.1 starts by assuming claim 1, so its constructed basis is not yet available under claim 2 alone. The missing inference is to apply the real or complex spectral theorem directly to the self-adjoint operator assumed in claim 2 and then use its assumed nonnegative eigenvalues. This is a short proof gap; the equivalence statement is sound.

seams_checked.note: Root linear-first pairing and Dirac outer-product conversion are retained in the Naimark calculations.
Density operators require nonzero spaces, nonnegativity, and trace one; complete positive families supply effects without assuming a measurement law.
Ancilla-last ordering, product pairing, finite product bases, and scalar-unit identifications match the suppliers.
Finite branch laws use instrument normalization and density only on positive-weight children; zero-weight descendants need no states.
Computational projectors are checked explicitly; Lüders maps are selected and validated before conditional coset states are used.
Readout explicitly selects Lüders branches; reference extensions use the actual block rule, and conditional outputs require positive weight.
Character-code outcome probabilities are calculated from rank-one density matrices and the projective trace rule, including invalid codes of weight zero.
Good/bad probabilities use orthogonal projections; positive conditional outputs and zero/unit endpoint conventions respect the supplier hypotheses.
Likelihood readouts use orthogonal good/bad projections and avoid normalizing impossible endpoint branches.
Marked tests explicitly specify Lüders instruments on all retained registers; compute/read/uncompute and positive-branch normalization are derived locally.
Basis projections and density hypotheses are established before applying projective probabilities; implementation costs remain separate.
Spectral readout uses projected squared norms and the explicitly selected QPE instrument; conditional states can retain multiple eigenspaces.
The coherent sampler law derives each probability by the projective trace rule and a rank-one trace calculation.
Observable effects are proved nonnegative and complete; amplified conditional outputs rely on an explicitly supplied flag-only instrument.
The QAOA example applies the computational projective law to its explicitly calculated normalized amplitudes.
Dihedral Fourier and pair-combination laws specify Lüders branches, calculate positive weights, and discard measured factors explicitly.
The Simon register instrument proves amplified positivity, trace preservation on every operator, and positive-only normalization.

Most uses preserve the finite POVM law. However, fixed-arity measurement synthesis [F4] attributes a flag-compression rule to the POVM Definition, which does not state it; the exact citation gap is recorded in alerts.
Identity-channel complete positivity and heralded positive/zero branch conventions agree with the definitions.
Swap-test projections and tensor-product repetition effects are established before applying the projective trace law.
The prepared evolution is shown to produce a density operator; success uses supplied finite POVM effects and accepting event sums.
Channel and Choi/Kraus uses retain all finite ancilla dimensions and the ancilla-last block convention.
Discrimination and variation use finite nonnegative complete effects; support restriction uses amplified positivity under inclusion and compression.
Global-phase comparisons construct valid density operators and POVMs before invoking their trace weights and normalization.
Instrument trace preservation is used on all operators; induced POVMs are proved separately, and deferred measurement respects block extensions and zero branches.
Acceptance weights are identified with a finite computational POVM on a density operator, including empty wire tuples as one-dimensional registers.
Pauli branches prove positivity for each finite block amplification and total trace preservation before claiming instrument status.
Outcome projections and normalized density operators are constructed explicitly; teleportation conditional branches have positive weight 1/4.
One-bit and transcript laws use projective trace weights, explicitly normalized positive branches, zero-output branches, and locally proved instrument completeness.
